 Shopee: A shopping paradise or a fertile ground for counterfeit goods?
 The discovery of nearly 7,000 counterfeit OMO and Lifebuoy products in Hanoi, along with authorities working with Shopee to verify sales data, continues to raise questions about the platform's ability to control counterfeit goods. When counterfeit products bearing well-known brand names can be sold online, are the platform's control measures truly effective enough to protect consumers?
 Báo Đại biểu Nhân dân • 26/10/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e Add Vietnam.vn on G o o g l e 0 From the case involving nearly 7,000 suspected counterfeit products to the transaction trail on Shopee.
 On October 21, 2026, Team No. 1 of the Hanoi Market Management Department conducted an inspection of a facility producing and selling laundry detergent and shower gel in An Khanh commune, Hanoi. The inspection revealed a large quantity of counterfeit OMO and Lifebuoy branded products being manufactured and packaged at the facility.
 Specifically, authorities discovered 6,425 bottles of Lifebuoy shower gel (800g), 385 bottles (720g), and 72 cans of OMO MATIC laundry detergent (3.6kg). In total, 6,882 finished products were found to be counterfeit versions of trademarks protected in Vietnam. 
 Evidence seized in the case (Photo: Market Management Department) In addition to finished goods, the facility also contained thousands of empty bottles, pump nozzles, labels, and various raw materials used in production and packaging. Notably, at the time of inspection, the facility did not have a business registration certificate.
 However, one of the most noteworthy details of the case lies not only in the quantity of goods discovered, but also in the business practices of the establishment.
 According to information released by market management authorities, Ms. Le Thi Cham, the owner of the establishment, used a Shopee account for business transactions. During the verification process, Market Management Team No. 1 contacted Shopee Co., Ltd. to verify the information of the related online sales account.
 Based on documents provided by Shopee and transaction history data, authorities determined that the total value of counterfeit OMO MATIC and Lifebuoy branded finished goods was over 597 million VND.
 This figure reflects the value of the discovered finished products, not the total revenue generated through Shopee.
 The fact that authorities had to verify data from the e-commerce platform shows that traces of online business activity are a significant part of the case. However, publicly available information has not clarified how long the involved store had been operating, the number of completed orders, the number of products sold, or the range of customers who had transacted with it.
 This is precisely the issue that needs further clarification. Because if a manufacturing facility produces thousands of products bearing counterfeit versions of famous brands while simultaneously using e-commerce platforms for business, the story is no longer just about production at a specific location, but also involves the ability to distribute goods in the digital environment.
 A warehouse might be discovered and inspected at a given time. But with products traded online, determining the actual quantity of goods reaching consumers requires continuous cross-referencing of sales, shipping, and payment data.
 The incident in An Khanh therefore raises a bigger question: How is Shopee controlling the sale of goods at risk of counterfeiting, and are current measures sufficient to detect anomalies before authorities intervene?
 When counterfeit goods find their way onto e-commerce platforms.
 The rapid development of e-commerce has significantly changed the way goods are bought and sold in Vietnam. Platforms like Shopee help sellers reach a wider customer base, reduce store operating costs, and facilitate more convenient transactions.
 However, these very advantages can also be exploited by those involved in the counterfeit trade.
 In traditional business models, sellers typically have to maintain a physical store, business location, or distribution system. With e-commerce, an individual can reach a large number of consumers through an online storefront, product images, and promotional programs.
 Buyers, meanwhile, primarily make decisions based on information displayed on the screen. Verifying the origin and actual quality of a product before payment or delivery is not always easy.
 For common consumer goods such as laundry detergent, shower gel, cosmetics, food, or household appliances, this risk is even more concerning. These are products that are purchased frequently, have high demand, and come from many familiar brands.
 You may also like A product with packaging similar to the genuine article, presented with eye-catching images and an attractive price, can make it difficult for consumers to distinguish the difference.
 Notably, the incident in Hanoi involved OMO and Lifebuoy, two brands with widespread market recognition. The discovery of thousands of counterfeit products bearing these brand names demonstrates that the risk of counterfeit goods is not limited to unfamiliar or less regulated items.
 In fact, the problem of counterfeit goods on e-commerce platforms is not a new story.
 Previously, the People's Representatives Newspaper reported on the situation where individuals exploited social media, livestreaming, and e-commerce platforms to promote, finalize orders, and distribute infringing goods. The items mentioned ranged from cosmetics and medicated oils to dietary supplements, shoes, and clothing bearing famous brand names.
 Some individuals even use terms like "rep 1:1," "like auth," or "super fake" to promote goods that mimic genuine products. The public use of these terms reflects the complexity of online businesses dealing in goods that infringe on intellectual property rights.
 Of particular concern is that the sale of counterfeit goods in the digital environment not only damages brands whose intellectual property rights are infringed, but also directly affects consumers and legitimate businesses.
 When goods of unknown origin or bearing signs of counterfeiting are introduced into the same trading environment as legitimate products, buyers face the risk of confusion, while law- abiding businesses may have to compete with sellers who do not bear the corresponding costs of production, inspection, and brand protection.
 In the long run, this situation could also erode confidence in the e-commerce environment.
 However, to assess whether Shopee is becoming a hub for counterfeit goods, specific data on the scale and frequency of violations on the platform is needed. Isolated incidents are warning signs, but not enough to determine the prevalence of counterfeit goods across the entire platform.
 Can Shopee avoid responsibility for controlling counterfeit goods?
 One of the most important issues raised by the An Khanh incident is the responsibility of the e-commerce platform operator.
 According to Decree No. 52/2013/ND-CP on e-commerce, amended and supplemented by Decree No. 85/2021/ND-CP, businesses providing e-commerce trading platform services have specific obligations in controlling and handling business practices that violate the law.
 Specifically, the operating unit must take timely action upon detecting or receiving reports of infringement; coordinate with intellectual property rights holders to review and remove infringing products; and support state management agencies in investigating and handling violations.
 The regulations also require the removal of information about goods and services that violate the law within 24 hours of receiving a request from the competent state management agency.
 For online ordering platforms, responsibilities also include storing transaction information and establishing a point of contact for providing information to facilitate inspection and handling of violations. In cases where legal conditions are met, the operating entity may also incur joint liability for damages if it violates related obligations and causes harm.
 Thus, the law not only places responsibility on those directly involved in the production and sale of counterfeit goods, but also stipulates the obligation to control, coordinate, and handle the issue for the platform's operating unit.
 In its operating regulations published on its support system, Shopee also mentions its responsibility to provide information about entities suspected of violating the law to state management agencies, update keywords as recommended by competent authorities, and receive and process feedback related to activities on the platform.
 The question is how effectively these mechanisms are implemented in practice.
 For example, for a store selling well-known branded products like OMO and Lifebuoy, what measures does Shopee use to verify the origin of the goods? When a seller uploads products in large quantities or at unusual prices, does the system have a mechanism to review, warn, or request additional documentation?
 If a vendor is reported for selling counterfeit goods, how long does the verification and processing take? After an account is processed, what measures does the platform take to prevent the same vendor from continuing to sell through another account?
 These are questions that are of practical relevance to consumers.
 You may also like Of course, the fact that a business is found to have counterfeit goods and is using a Shopee account does not automatically mean that Shopee has violated the law. To determine the platform's responsibility in a specific case, it is necessary to clarify what information was posted for sale, when the platform became aware of or received reports of the alleged violation, and what corrective measures were taken.
 However, just because the seller is directly responsible for the goods does not mean that the role of the platform in maintaining a transparent and secure trading environment should be overlooked.
 As e-commerce platforms become a crucial link in connecting sellers and buyers, the ability to detect, prevent, and handle counterfeit goods must be considered one of the criteria for evaluating the quality of the platform's operations.
 In fact, from September 16th to October 15th, 2026, Hanoi's market management force detected and handled 229 violations during the peak period of combating intellectual property infringement, and transferred 3 cases with criminal implications to the investigative agency. The agency also determined to continue strengthening inspections and handling violations in e-commerce and online activities.
 These moves indicate that anti-counterfeiting efforts are being intensified, but they also highlight the need for closer coordination between regulatory agencies, intellectual property rights holders, and e-commerce platform operators.
 Regarding the case involving nearly 7,000 products suspected of being counterfeit OMO and Lifebuoy in Hanoi, market management forces have transferred the file to the police for further investigation into the alleged infringement of industrial property rights under Article 226 of the Penal Code.
 The results of the investigation will serve as the basis for determining the nature of the incident, the scale of the operation, and the responsibility of the individuals and organizations involved.
 However, the incident also highlights the need for greater transparency regarding the results of counterfeit control on e-commerce platforms, including Shopee. Data on stores found to be infringing, products removed, complaint processing times, and the ability to prevent sellers from reoffending will provide the public with a basis for realistically assessing the effectiveness of consumer protection measures.
 Because what consumers need is not just for counterfeit goods to be detected and dealt with after they appear on the market, but more importantly, for those products to be stopped before they reach the buyer.
 And until the ability to control counterfeit goods in the online environment is proven by transparent results, the question of whether Shopee is becoming a "haven" for counterfeit goods remains a matter of concern for regulatory agencies, businesses, and consumers.
